The Franco-American Alliance. A military alliance between France and the American revolutionaries during the American War of Independence, formally established in seventeen seventy-eight. French military support, naval power, and financial resources proved decisive in American victory and reshaped global geopolitics by weakening Britain's dominance.

The alliance began informally in seventeen seventy-five as France supplied covert military aid and supplies to American rebels including gunpowder, weapons, and uniforms, escalating to formal alliance after the American victory at Saratoga in seventeen seventy-seven. The victory at Saratoga convinced King Louis the Sixteenth and his ministers that American victory was possible, shifting France from cautious supplier to committed military partner. Benjamin Franklin played a crucial diplomatic role in Paris, cultivating French support through charm and deliberate cultivation of influential salon hosts and nobles. Franklin successfully negotiated the Treaty of Alliance in seventeen seventy-eight and the Treaty of Commerce, formal documents binding France and America against Britain. French military involvement included troops—the Comte de Rochambeau's expeditionary force of approximately six thousand men—naval forces, and artillery, filling critical American gaps in training and equipment. The Comte de Rochambeau coordinated operations with George Washington and proved instrumental in sieges like Yorktown, demonstrating sophisticated joint operations. The alliance turned the tide decisively; American forces alone could not have defeated the British without French intervention and naval superiority, particularly in preventing British reinforcement. French naval victories restricted British reinforcement and supply lines, particularly critical at Yorktown in seventeen eighty-one, where the French navy blockaded British escape. The alliance created a debt burden that contributed to France's fiscal crisis—approximately one point three billion livres—and ultimately to the French Revolution a decade later, as France taxed its people to pay war costs. The Franco-American Alliance connects to the American Revolution as the conflict the alliance enabled the Americans to win; France as the European power that became America's critical ally; Benjamin Franklin as the diplomat who secured French support in Paris; the Battle of Saratoga as the American victory that convinced France to commit formally; the Battle of Yorktown as the decisive siege where French forces proved essential; the British Empire as the power whose dominance the alliance challenged; and the Comte de Rochambeau as the French commander of expeditionary forces in America.
